newsitem.title: BELGIUM: FOCUS-Optimism grows over EMU budget pact deal.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Optimism grows over EMU budget pact deal.

text.p: European Union policy-makers voiced optimism on Wednesday that differences over a budget stability pact for countries joining monetary union could be resolved in time for an EU summit in Amsterdam next week.

France's Socialist-led government on Monday threw Europe's single currency project into confusion when it asked for more time to consider the stability pact, a measure designed to keep the spending of single currency nations under control.
Adressing the concerns of the French electorate, Prime Minister Lionel Jospin has maintained the budget accord must be balanced by an equally tough commitment to boosting jobs across Europe.

France's position has prompted worries over the timetable for economic and monetary union, with most governments unwilling to revisit an accord agreed in principle last December after lengthy and often fractious negotiations.
EU officials were confident, however, that a deal could be struck to accomodate French demands and allow the budget pact to be signed by EU leaders in Amsterdam on June 16 and 17.
"I believe that an accord is still possible for Amsterdam and if it is not possible for Amsterdam, it will be right after," Italian Foreign Minister Lamberto Dini told reporters in Rome.

Signalling a desire to alleviate the concerns of its 14 European partners, France's finance minister Dominique Strauss-Kahn said the government wanted an early solution but insisted it must win its demand for a greater focus on jobs and economic growth.

"We are clearly going to find a solution," Strauss-Kahn said after the weekly cabinet meeting. "If we can move forward quickly, it is obviously better. No one wants to drag things out for the sake of it."
A series of high-level diplomatic meetings between now and the EU summit are expected to lead to a political resolution that would address France's demands.

Optimism over a solution to the diplomatic impasse first surfaced on Tuesday when Dutch Prime Minister Wim Kok said Jospin had told him that he could agree to the stability pact before he presented his economic policies to parliament on June 19.

Responding to Kok's remarks, European Commission President Jacques Santer, who is due to meet the French government on Thursday, told a news conference in the French city of Strasbourg that he was confident of a near-term solution.
"From what I know as a result of the meeting with Wim Kok and Mr Jospin...it would seem based on these discussions we can succeed in Amsterdam," Santer said.

EU diplomats said the symbolic value of an agreement on the accord and its importance in sustaining the momentum behind the single currency was more important than the actual signatures of 15 heads of state.

Echoing the upbeat turn of events, German Foreign Minister Klaus Kinkel said France remained committed to the budgetary accord and indicated that Germany was prepared to agree to a jobs chapter in negotiations to amend the Maastricht Treaty.
"It (France) will adhere to the stability pact and -- just like the German government -- it will launch the euro on time according to the stability criteria," Kinkel said in a prepared speech.
The German minister stressed, however, that Bonn would not accept "unaccountable" or expensive jobs programmes to boost the job prospects of the 18 million unemployed in the EU.

Debate over the stability pact is particularly sensitive in Germany, which sees the new French government's initiatives as a potential threat to the credibility of the euro and a future European Central Bank.
Germany and France will hold bilateral talks in Poiters in western France on Friday.
